title: The Next 100 Years: A Forecast for the 21st Century
author: George Friedman
vetoReason: The central century-long forecast depends on selected geopolitical constraints being sufficiently determinative to predict detailed events. Forecasting specialist Philip Tetlock, in the review excerpt reproduced by international-relations scholar Daniel Drezner, criticizes its reliance on privileged pundit judgment rather than demonstrated predictive method. The criticism concerns the book's foundation; acknowledging that details may be wrong does not resolve it.
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Speculative nonfiction is not fiction merely because scenarios are implausible. V9 applies to the forecasting foundation, not to the existence of forecasting as a genre. Friedman explains in his Carnegie Council remarks that the purpose is to identify durable forces; Kirkus finds useful geopolitical reasoning. These defenses support subsidiary value but do not validate the detailed forecast. Global influence prevents an automatic US-only deduction; geopolitics and war are central, T12=-10. No historical endpoint deduction for future scenarios. Not selected for praise.
notes: Geographic and demographic facts are mixed with weakly validated inference to detailed future events.
Connects geography, population, technology, economic resources and military power.
Some useful constraint-based questions, but highly specific scenarios are unsafe as planning assumptions.
Describes strategic incentives but often treats constraints as sufficient causes of particular outcomes.
D=6, moderate confidence from Kirkus, Publishers Weekly, the author talk and reader reports. Early comparisons add learning; extended imagined wars add less reliable explanatory value.
Underlying geography persists; forecast-dependent value decays as assumptions and events change.
Strategic risk and technological capability fit, though power competition dominates.
Experienced analyst; relevant forecasting specialists challenge the method.
An accessible chronological scenario, with narrative certainty stronger than warranted.
Clear prose but excessive specificity and confident transitions.

title: The Next Decade: Where We've Been ... and Where We're Going
author: George Friedman
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. A strategic policy argument and dated forecast, not technical training. Korstanje's detailed review criticizes ethnocentric premises but also recognizes useful observations. A US policy perspective alone does not establish V2 or V6, and criticism of another Friedman book is not automatically transferred as a veto here. Inspected evidence does not establish a serious veto with sufficient confidence. Global consequences, not local US history, dominate; T11=0. Power and politics are central, T12=-10. The 2011 forecast is retained as a historical argument, not current guidance; no H13 deduction because its organizing period was prospective. Not selected on praise.
notes: Strategic judgments rest heavily on interpretation and selected history rather than calibrated forecasts.
Connects trade, security, domestic institutions and international balances.
Useful questions about limits of power and competing objectives, with context-dependent prescriptions.
Explains some incentive conflicts; causal necessity and national preferences are often asserted.

title: Flashpoints: The Emerging Crisis in Europe
author: George Friedman
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Comparative European history and geopolitical analysis, not single-nation history or a specialist curriculum. Tangredi praises the historical explanation in Naval War College Review. Reader reports identify sweeping national generalizations, uneven structure and thin documentation; these limit confidence without proving a serious veto. No automatic transfer of the veto on The Next 100 Years. Political and military conflict dominate, T12=-10; cross-European scope means T11=0. History supports contemporary and prospective claims, with no single closed endpoint. Mixed reader reception prevents quota selection.
notes: Historical reporting offers context, but some national-character claims and intentions are insufficiently substantiated.
Connects borders, economic tensions, institutions, migration and conflict.
Useful map of recurring constraints and regional vulnerabilities, with limited forecast reliability.
Explains geographic pressures but can overstate continuity from past conflict to future action.

title: Disunited Nations: The Scramble for Power in an Ungoverned World
author: Peter Zeihan
vetoReason: The recurring forecast assumes that US withdrawal necessarily ends the international order and produces a largely ungoverned world. International-relations scholar Herman Salton directly identifies this foundational simplification and the assumed rather than established condition of non-governance. Country-level geographic detail does not establish that central causal chain. Favorable reception of the book's exposition does not resolve this criticism.
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Same work as the source's alternate subtitle Succeeding in a World Where No One Gets Along; not Sean Byrnes's distinct book. Speculative nonfiction passes hard exclusions. V9 concerns the causal foundation rather than a particular political position or prediction. Kirkus strongly praises the geographic and demographic account; the useful comparative material is retained in the counterfactual score. World-wide consequences prevent T11; geopolitical power is central, T12=-10. No H13 for forward scenarios. Not selected despite high reader ratings.
notes: Geographic and demographic information is mixed with unsupported necessity in the central collapse narrative.
Connects energy, population, trade access, geography and security in country comparisons.
Useful prompts for resource and supply-chain vulnerability, but deterministic forecasts are unreliable planning inputs.
Several constraints are explained; alternative institutional responses receive inadequate causal weight.
D=7, moderate confidence from Salton's review extract, Kirkus and readers. Country cases contribute distinct constraints, though repeated collapse framing reduces yield.
Structural data retain value; confident near-term scenarios and global-order assumptions age quickly.
Trade, logistics, resources and strategic risk fit well despite the political center.
Experienced geopolitical consultant; specialist criticism targets the main framework.
Clear country portraits and vivid writing support accessibility.
Categorical and theatrical formulations often conceal uncertainty.
